Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The design was developed via a design probe and interview sessions with an autistic adult self-advocate (disabled stakeholder) but is explicitly framed as technology aimed at the public at large to reduce social stigma (diverse stakeholders including non-disabled public). The goal is both celebratory/engaging (fun, positive self-presentation via a disco ball collage of interests and traits) and utilitarian (reducing stigma, improving first impressions and social understanding). This aligns best with a design that considers both fun and utility from the outset with diverse stakeholders in mind.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) unstructured play (i.e., no rules, making art),
        (2) semi-structured play (i.e., playground activities),
        (3) flexible structure with rules (i.e., improv),
        (4) flexible game (i.e., board game with house rules),
        (5) game with rigid rules (i.e., video game)
reasoning: The study is a design probe and co-design session to create a celebratory profile-image technology, not a game. There is no mention of rules, gameplay, or structured play activities; the interaction is open-ended interviewing and brainstorming about designs, closest to unstructured creative activity rather than any form of game or play with rules.

        (1) entirely skill-based (i.e., trivia, sports),
        (2) mostly skill-based (i.e., mario kart),
        (3) equally skill and chance-based (i.e., catan),
        (4) mostly chance-based (i.e., Uno),
        (5) entirely chance-based (i.e., all dice)
reasoning: The study is a design probe for a customizable profile-image/disco ball interface to represent personal traits and interests; there is no game, contest, or probabilistic mechanism. Any user outcome depends entirely on their choices and input, making it effectively entirely skill/choice-based rather than involving chance.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely solo (i.e., solitaire),
        (2) mostly solo (i.e., playing against AI in single-player StarCraft),
        (3) mix of solo and social affordances (i.e., animal crossing),
        (4) mostly social, but aspects are independent (i.e., house on hill haunt transition),
        (5) entirely social (i.e., tag)
reasoning: The designed technology is a customizable disco ball profile image used in social contexts like Zoom to shape first impressions and support high-quality contact. It is not a solo game-like activity, but a representational tool embedded in social interaction, with independent customization by each user and social interpretation by others. This aligns best with a mix of solo (individual configuration) and social affordances (use in social platforms), i.e., option 3.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: The study is a design probe for a celebratory profile-image technology (a disco ball collage) used in contexts like Zoom. There is no notion of turns, steps, or phased actions between multiple players; interaction is essentially individual and not turn-structured. Among the given options, this best aligns with an entirely simultaneous interaction model.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely synchronous (i.e., real time strategy game),
        (2) mostly synchronous with a few asynchronous affordances (i.e., league of legends),
        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),
        (5) entirely asynchronous (i.e., chess by postage mail)
reasoning: The described technology is a customizable disco-ball style profile image used in contexts like Zoom. It is configured through interviews and design sessions, and then functions as a static or slowly changing profile representation rather than a real-time interactive system. There is no indication of real-time multiplayer or synchronous interaction mechanics; the affordance is essentially asynchronous self-presentation.

        (1) entirely competitive (i.e., spit card game),
        (2) mostly competitive, but sometimes collaboration is important (i.e., forbidden island),
        (3) mix of competitive and collaborative (i.e., mario party 2 vs 2 mini-games),
        (4) mostly collaborative (i.e., animal crossing),
        (5) entirely collaborative (i.e., pandemic)
reasoning: The work is a design probe for a celebratory profile-image technology to reduce stigma and improve first impressions in contexts like Zoom. There is no game or competitive mechanic; the technology is meant to support understanding, awareness, and appreciation of neurodiversity among users. This is fully oriented toward mutual support and positive social interaction rather than any form of competition, so it best fits an entirely collaborative design.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The core design is a customizable disco ball profile icon used by anyone in a classroom/Zoom context, with each user having the same type of artifact (12 tiles, traits/experiences encoded as colors). There are no distinct roles, abilities, or mechanics that differ between participants; everyone interacts with the same kind of representation. This makes the interaction structure entirely symmetrical rather than role- or ability-asymmetrical.
